timeline.subject: For Approval: Microsoft Permissive License
timeline.snippet: Recommends OSI approval of MS-PL despite similarity to existing permissive licenses, arguing that encouraging Microsoft to use an OSI-approved license is valuable in itself.
timeline.point_zh: 建议 OSI 批准 MS-PL，尽管它与已有的宽松许可证类似，但鼓励微软采用 OSI 批准的许可证就本身很有价值。
timeline.point: Recommends OSI approval of MS-PL despite similarity to existing permissive licenses, arguing that encouraging Microsoft to use an OSI-approved license is valuable in itself.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Microsoft Permissive License
timeline.snippet: Defends the only under this license clause, arguing that wanting code to remain under a permissive license is a legitimate goal, and noting the asymmetry in how copyleft vs permissive preferences are treated.
timeline.point_zh: 为“仅限本许可证”条款辩护，认为希望代码保持在宽松许可证下是合理诉求，指出社区对 copyleft 和宽松许可证的偏好存在不对等态度。
timeline.point: Defends the only under this license clause, arguing that wanting code to remain under a permissive license is a legitimate goal, and noting the asymmetry in how copyleft vs permissive preferences are treated.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Microsoft Permissive License
timeline.snippet: Argues that MS-PL is incompatible with GPL v2 because GPL v2 does not allow patent retaliation clauses, while MS-PL, GPL v3, and Apache 2.0 all include such provisions.
timeline.point_zh: 认为 MS-PL 与 GPL v2 不兼容，因为 GPL v2 不允许专利报复条款，而 MS-PL、GPL v3 和 Apache 2.0 都包含此类条款。
timeline.point: Argues that MS-PL is incompatible with GPL v2 because GPL v2 does not allow patent retaliation clauses, while MS-PL, GPL v3, and Apache 2.0 all include such provisions.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Microsoft Permissive License
timeline.snippet: Discusses sublicensing law, arguing that BSD-style licenses are direct grants from the author to anyone possessing the software, making the sublicensing question largely moot.
timeline.point_zh: 讨论分许可法律问题，认为 BSD 风格许可证是作者直接授予任何持有软件者的授权，分许可问题在很大程度上不成立。
timeline.point: Discusses sublicensing law, arguing that BSD-style licenses are direct grants from the author to anyone possessing the software, making the sublicensing question largely moot.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Microsoft Permissive License
timeline.snippet: Argues that incorporating BSD-licensed code into a GPL project creates a dual-licensed work (GPL portions + BSD portions), not a purely GPL project, and that the SFLC article is being misread.
timeline.point_zh: 认为将 BSD 许可代码纳入 GPL 项目会创建双重许可作品（GPL 部分 + BSD 部分），而非纯粹的 GPL 项目，指出 SFLC 文章被误读了。
timeline.point: Argues that incorporating BSD-licensed code into a GPL project creates a dual-licensed work (GPL portions + BSD portions), not a purely GPL project, and that the SFLC article is being misread.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Microsoft Permissive License
timeline.snippet: Analyzes potential trademark issues with a hypothetical logo program for MS-PL, noting it could require license changes and raise discrimination concerns under OSI rules.
timeline.point_zh: 分析了为 MS-PL 设立标志认证计划可能带来的商标问题，指出这可能需要修改许可证并引发 OSI 规则下的歧视问题。
timeline.point: Analyzes potential trademark issues with a hypothetical logo program for MS-PL, noting it could require license changes and raise discrimination concerns under OSI rules.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Microsoft Permissive License
timeline.snippet: Dismisses the trademark concerns as speculative, noting the MS-PL trademark situation is the same as other OSI-approved licenses, and sees no obstacles to approval.
timeline.point_zh: 驳斥商标担忧为推测性的，指出 MS-PL 的商标情况与其他 OSI 批准的许可证相同，认为批准不存在障碍。
timeline.point: Dismisses the trademark concerns as speculative, noting the MS-PL trademark situation is the same as other OSI-approved licenses, and sees no obstacles to approval.

timeline.point: The FSF lawyer raises a clarification question about ASL2's patent retaliation clause and GPL compatibility: when a user makes a defensive patent claim against Apache, whether the patent license for the GPL portion and the ASL portion of the combined work is withdrawn or remains in force.

timeline.snippet: Points out that if the interpretation of the patent grant is correct, then ASL2 would not be a free software license at all, illustrating the logic behind FSF's position.

board_vote.motion_text: Fair License – modification to existing OSI approved license — we approve

timeline.subject: For Approval: Fair License
timeline.snippet: Submits the Fair License as a generalized BSD-style license with an explicit Due Credit requirement (retention and notification of the instrument), believing it is OSD-compliant and compatible with most other licenses.

timeline.point: Submits the Fair License as a generalized BSD-style license with an explicit Due Credit requirement (retention and notification of the instrument), believing it is OSD-compliant and compatible with most other licenses.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Fair License
timeline.snippet: Proposes simplifying the Fair License by removing superfluous definitions, shortening the disclaimer, implying attribution BSD-style, and dropping the explicit acceptance clause, keeping only essentials.
timeline.point_zh: 提议简化 Fair License：删除多余定义、缩短免责声明、以 BSD 方式隐含署名、删除明示接受条款，仅保留核心内容。
timeline.point: Proposes simplifying the Fair License by removing superfluous definitions, shortening the disclaimer, implying attribution BSD-style, and dropping the explicit acceptance clause, keeping only essentials.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Fair License
timeline.snippet: Provides a newer Fair License text to replace the posted version, mainly removing a soon-dead rhid.com/fair link and switching 'usage' to 'use'.
timeline.point_zh: 提供新版 Fair License 以替换已发布版本，主要删除即将失效的 rhid.com/fair 链接并将 usage 改为 use。
timeline.point: Provides a newer Fair License text to replace the posted version, mainly removing a soon-dead rhid.com/fair link and switching 'usage' to 'use'.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Fair License
timeline.snippet: Worries that the Fair License's use of "use" does not clearly cover modification or distribution, unlike BSD which lists them explicitly.
timeline.point_zh: 担忧 Fair License 用「use」一词未能明确涵盖修改与分发，而 BSD 许可证则逐一明列。
timeline.point: Worries that the Fair License's use of "use" does not clearly cover modification or distribution, unlike BSD which lists them explicitly.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Fair License
timeline.snippet: Remarks that the parties still have to choose (regarding the Fair License scope question).
timeline.point_zh: 指出当事人仍须做出选择（针对 Fair License 范围之争）。
timeline.point: Remarks that the parties still have to choose (regarding the Fair License scope question).

timeline.subject: For Approval: Fair License

timeline.point: Asks the list to indicate what wording they consider correct for the Fair License.

submissions.name: The OCLC Research Public License 2.0 License
aliases: discuss: OCLC Office of Research Open Source License

osi_api.name: The OCLC Research Public License 2.0 License

timeline.subject: discuss: OCLC Office of Research Open Source License
timeline.snippet: Submits the OCLC Office of Research Public License 2.0 for OSI certification, explaining it is a reworking of ORPL 1.0 based on the OSD and MPL with various simplifications.
timeline.point_zh: 提交 OCLC 办公室研究公共许可证 2.0 申请 OSI 认证，说明这是基于 OSD 和 MPL 对 ORPL 1.0 的重新编写，包含多处简化。
timeline.point: Submits the OCLC Office of Research Public License 2.0 for OSI certification, explaining it is a reworking of ORPL 1.0 based on the OSD and MPL with various simplifications.

timeline.subject: discuss: OCLC Office of Research Open Source License
timeline.snippet: Finds the ORPL 2.0 generally OSD-compliant but raises concerns about the overlapping grant clauses in Sections 1 and 4, questioning the legal basis for Section 4 surviving termination.
timeline.point_zh: 认为 ORPL 2.0 基本符合 OSD，但对第 1 条和第 4 条之间重叠的授权条款提出疑虑，质疑第 4 条在许可终止后继续有效的法律依据。
timeline.point: Finds the ORPL 2.0 generally OSD-compliant but raises concerns about the overlapping grant clauses in Sections 1 and 4, questioning the legal basis for Section 4 surviving termination.

timeline.subject: discuss: OCLC Office of Research Open Source License
timeline.snippet: Questions whether the Combined Work definition in ORPL 2.0 is precise enough to exclude aggregate works, arguing that as written the restrictions would apply to CD compilations and thus violate the OSD.
timeline.point_zh: 质疑 ORPL 2.0 中合并作品的定义是否足够精确以排除汇编作品，认为按现有措辞限制条款将适用于 CD 合集，因此不符合 OSD。
timeline.point: Questions whether the Combined Work definition in ORPL 2.0 is precise enough to exclude aggregate works, arguing that as written the restrictions would apply to CD compilations and thus violate the OSD.

timeline.subject: discuss: OCLC Office of Research Open Source License
timeline.snippet: Acknowledges OCLC's intent with 'modifiable code' aligns with the OSD but agrees the Combined Work vs. Aggregate Work distinction in Section 3.D is unclear and suggests using 'derivative work' terminology.
timeline.point_zh: 认可 OCLC 对'可修改代码'的使用意图符合 OSD，但同意第 3.D 条中合并作品与汇编作品的区别不清晰，建议使用'演绎作品'术语来消除歧义。
timeline.point: Acknowledges OCLC's intent with 'modifiable code' aligns with the OSD but agrees the Combined Work vs. Aggregate Work distinction in Section 3.D is unclear and suggests using 'derivative work' terminology.

timeline.subject: discuss: OCLC Office of Research Open Source License
timeline.snippet: Responds to feedback on modifiable code by noting Java bytecode can be decompiled, acknowledges the need to clarify the modifiable code definition, and confirms they will revisit the Combined Work vs. Aggregate Work distinction.
timeline.point_zh: 回应关于可修改代码的反馈，指出 Java 字节码可以通过反编译器还原，承认需要澄清可修改代码的定义，并确认将重新审视合并作品与汇编作品的区别。
timeline.point: Responds to feedback on modifiable code by noting Java bytecode can be decompiled, acknowledges the need to clarify the modifiable code definition, and confirms they will revisit the Combined Work vs. Aggregate Work distinction.

timeline.subject: discuss: OCLC Office of Research Open Source License
timeline.snippet: Points out that defining the Original Contributor as the OCLC Office of Research prevents third parties from independently using the license for their own software, as OCLC cannot grant rights it does not hold.
timeline.point_zh: 指出将原始贡献者定义为 OCLC 研究办公室会导致第三方无法独立将其用于自己的软件，因为 OCLC 无法授予自己不拥有的权利。
timeline.point: Points out that defining the Original Contributor as the OCLC Office of Research prevents third parties from independently using the license for their own software, as OCLC cannot grant rights it does not hold.

timeline.subject: discuss: OCLC Office of Research Open Source License
timeline.snippet: Acknowledges that Sections 1 and 4 overlap and cause confusion, agrees to seek improvements, and confirms they will revisit Section 3.D in response to reviewer feedback.
timeline.point_zh: 承认第 1 条和第 4 条部分重叠并导致授权范围的困惑，同意寻求改进，并确认将重新审视第 3.D 条。
timeline.point: Acknowledges that Sections 1 and 4 overlap and cause confusion, agrees to seek improvements, and confirms they will revisit Section 3.D in response to reviewer feedback.

timeline.subject: discuss: OCLC Office of Research Open Source License
timeline.snippet: Draws a parallel between Java bytecode obfuscation/de-obfuscation and the historical cat-and-mouse game of copy-protected diskettes, implying the modifiability argument is fragile.
timeline.point_zh: 将 Java 字节码的混淆与反混淆比作早期复制保护软盘的猫鼠游戏，暗示可修改性的论点较为脆弱。
timeline.point: Draws a parallel between Java bytecode obfuscation/de-obfuscation and the historical cat-and-mouse game of copy-protected diskettes, implying the modifiability argument is fragile.

timeline.subject: discuss: OCLC Office of Research Open Source License
timeline.snippet: States the ORPL 2.0 appears OSD-compliant apart from issues already raised, and would support approval once those issues are clarified.
timeline.point_zh: 认为 ORPL 2.0 除已提出的问题外基本符合 OSD，一旦这些问题得到澄清，将支持该许可证被纳入 OSI 批准许可证库。

timeline.point: Clarifies that the AFL requires no sublicensing and imposes no restrictions on offering additional warranty terms, addressing concerns about commercial sublicensing models.

timeline.subject: Academic Free License

timeline.subject: NCSA Open Source License
timeline.snippet: Argues that existing MIT license variants must be retained because too many people already use them to expect a mass migration.
timeline.point_zh: 主张必须保留现有 MIT 许可证变体，因为使用者太多，不能期望大规模变更。
timeline.point: Argues that existing MIT license variants must be retained because too many people already use them to expect a mass migration.

timeline.subject: NCSA Open Source License
timeline.snippet: Corrects Bruce Perens' count, noting that unifying MIT variants would result in three licenses rather than one.
timeline.point_zh: 纠正 Bruce Perens 的说法，指出统一 MIT 变体实际上是三种许可证而非一种。
timeline.point: Corrects Bruce Perens' count, noting that unifying MIT variants would result in three licenses rather than one.

timeline.subject: NCSA Open Source License
timeline.snippet: States that OSI will approve NCSA if it meets the OSD, though they will try to convince submitters to use existing licenses first.
timeline.point_zh: 表示 OSI 会按 OSD 标准批准 NCSA 许可证，虽然会先尝试说服提交者使用现有许可证。
timeline.point: States that OSI will approve NCSA if it meets the OSD, though they will try to convince submitters to use existing licenses first.

timeline.subject: NCSA Open Source License
timeline.snippet: Distinguishes between trademark protection and obnoxious advertising clauses. Supports trademark-protecting licenses but insists trademark names should use template placeholders to avoid needing separate approvals for each variation.
timeline.point_zh: 区分商标保护与侵入式广告条款。支持保护商标的许可证，但坚持商标名应使用模板占位符，避免为每个变体单独审批。
timeline.point: Distinguishes between trademark protection and obnoxious advertising clauses. Supports trademark-protecting licenses but insists trademark names should use template placeholders to avoid needing separate approvals for each variation.

timeline.subject: NCSA Open Source License
timeline.snippet: Explains that Apache's new advertising clause is GPL-compatible, but the restriction on naming derivative works remains FSF-incompatible.
timeline.point_zh: 说明 Apache 的新广告条款与 GPL 兼容，但对衍生作品命名的限制仍与 FSF 不兼容。
timeline.point: Explains that Apache's new advertising clause is GPL-compatible, but the restriction on naming derivative works remains FSF-incompatible.

timeline.subject: NCSA Open Source License
timeline.snippet: Clarifies that AbiWord code can be used like any GPL code, but certain expressions and artwork are not freely reusable.
timeline.point_zh: 澄清 AbiWord 代码可以像其他 GPL 代码一样使用，但某些表达和艺术作品不能自由再利用。
timeline.point: Clarifies that AbiWord code can be used like any GPL code, but certain expressions and artwork are not freely reusable.

timeline.subject: NCSA Open Source License
timeline.snippet: Clarifies that while no one needs a separate trademark license, a licensor cannot grant trademark rights for derivative works through a general open source license.
timeline.point_zh: 澄清虽然不需要单独的商标许可证，但许可方不能通过通用开源许可证授予衍生作品使用商标的权利。
timeline.point: Clarifies that while no one needs a separate trademark license, a licensor cannot grant trademark rights for derivative works through a general open source license.

timeline.subject: OSI API submission record: The X.Net, Inc. License
timeline.snippet: (OSI API records Carl W. Brown - Russell Nelson as the submitter of The X.Net, Inc. License. The public mailing-list archive does not expose a concrete submission message for this event.)
timeline.point: (OSI API records Carl W. Brown - Russell Nelson as the submitter of The X.Net, Inc. License. The public mailing-list archive does not expose a concrete submission message for this event.)
timeline.point_zh: （OSI API 记录 Carl W. Brown - Russell Nelson 为 The X.Net, Inc. License 的提交者；公开邮件归档没有暴露这一事件的具体提交邮件。）

timeline.subject: X.Net, Inc. License
timeline.snippet: Asks whether the X.Net license qualifies as open source.
timeline.point_zh: 询问 X.Net 许可证是否属于开源许可证。
timeline.point: Asks whether the X.Net license qualifies as open source.

timeline.subject: X.Net, Inc. License
timeline.snippet: Says the X.Net license appears to satisfy the open-source definition, though it is basically MIT plus a jurisdiction clause and should ideally be replaced with an existing approved license.
timeline.point_zh: 表示 X.Net 许可证看起来符合开源定义，不过它本质上是 MIT 加上管辖条款，最好还是改用现有已批准的许可证。
timeline.point: Says the X.Net license appears to satisfy the open-source definition, though it is basically MIT plus a jurisdiction clause and should ideally be replaced with an existing approved license.

timeline.subject: X.Net, Inc. License
timeline.snippet: Questions the value of the jurisdiction clause, prefers plain-text submissions, and warns that another MIT-like variant adds needless license proliferation and compliance overhead.
timeline.point_zh: 质疑管辖条款的价值，倾向于纯文本提交，并警告再增加一个类似 MIT 的变体会带来不必要的许可证泛滥和合规负担。
timeline.point: Questions the value of the jurisdiction clause, prefers plain-text submissions, and warns that another MIT-like variant adds needless license proliferation and compliance overhead.

timeline.subject: X.Net, Inc. License
timeline.snippet: Argues that specifying jurisdiction is common, does not conflict with open-source intent, and is not a valid reason to reject the license.
timeline.point_zh: 主张指定管辖地很常见，不与开源精神冲突，也不应成为拒绝该许可证的理由。
timeline.point: Argues that specifying jurisdiction is common, does not conflict with open-source intent, and is not a valid reason to reject the license.

timeline.subject: X.Net, Inc. License
timeline.snippet: Warns that licenses with different jurisdiction clauses may be mutually incompatible, which is a problem.
timeline.point_zh: 警告说带有不同管辖条款的许可证彼此之间可能不兼容，这是个问题。
timeline.point: Warns that licenses with different jurisdiction clauses may be mutually incompatible, which is a problem.

timeline.subject: X.Net, Inc. License
timeline.snippet: Asks whether the claimed GPL incompatibility comes from GPL's ban on additional conditions.
timeline.point_zh: 询问所谓与 GPL 不兼容，是否是因为 GPL 禁止附加条件。
timeline.point: Asks whether the claimed GPL incompatibility comes from GPL's ban on additional conditions.

timeline.subject: X.Net, Inc. License
timeline.snippet: Reports that the GPL-compatibility objection is theoretical and not intuitively persuasive, but notes RMS treats it as a real problem.
timeline.point_zh: 表示关于 GPL 兼容性的异议更多是理论上的、直觉上并不强，但 RMS 认为这确实是个问题。
timeline.point: Reports that the GPL-compatibility objection is theoretical and not intuitively persuasive, but notes RMS treats it as a real problem.

timeline.subject: X.Net, Inc. License
timeline.snippet: Explains that the GPL concern is about parties choosing a venue where copyright law might undermine GPL enforcement.
timeline.point_zh: 解释说，对 GPL 的担忧在于有人可能选择一个会削弱 GPL 执行效果的司法辖区。
timeline.point: Explains that the GPL concern is about parties choosing a venue where copyright law might undermine GPL enforcement.

timeline.snippet: Greetings, My name is Ken Sedgwick. I am a volunteer package maintainer working to get the ACE and TAO software libraries into standard Linux distribution. I am not a lawyer. The
timeline.point: Submits the ACE License for OSI certification to allow the ACE and TAO software libraries into Linux distributions.

timeline.subject: For Approval: ACE License
timeline.snippet: Ken Sedgwick scripsit: > My name is Ken Sedgwick. I am a volunteer package maintainer working > to get the ACE and TAO software libraries into standard Linux > distribution. I am
timeline.point: Argues the license is obviously Open Source, meets all OSD clauses, and should be approved immediately.

timeline.subject: For Approval: ACE License
timeline.snippet: Ken Sedgwick wrote: > The plain text copy of the license is attached to this message. I recommend withholding approval until all of the following are changed: 1. The license inclu
timeline.point: Recommends withholding approval until restrictive clauses, URL references, Y2K claims, contradictory support statements, and indemnification paragraphs are changed.

timeline.subject: For Approval: ACE License
timeline.snippet: Forrest J. Cavalier III scripsit: > I recommend withholding approval until all of the following are > changed: A meta-point: note that this license is actually in use for software
timeline.point: Counters previous criticisms, arguing that the license is permissive, in active use, and does not restrict use or reuse as claimed.

timeline.subject: For Approval: ACE License
timeline.snippet: John Cowan wrote in part: > Forrest J. Cavalier III scripsit: >>1. The license includes a statement whiich I think is a restriction >> on use.... >> You must, however, >> include
timeline.point: Argues that 'built using' does not imply 'derived from' and that the license on tools should not cover the output.

timeline.subject: For Approval: ACE License
timeline.snippet: Forrest J. Cavalier III scripsit: > Compilers and linkers build software, and the license on the tools > does not cover the output the way this license tries to. > > "Built using"
timeline.point: Disagrees with the interpretation of 'built with', asserting that programs are built with libraries, not just compilers or linkers.

timeline.subject: For Approval: ACE License
timeline.snippet: If this license cannot be revised, I recommend that OSI withhold approval. With a minor revision, I world agree that approval is warranted. The second paragraph should be revised.
timeline.point: Recommends withholding approval if the license cannot be revised, citing concerns that the second paragraph may violate OSD articles by allowing proprietary distribution.

license_texts.text:
| Copyback License (Draft 4)
| 
|  Redistribution and use, with or without modification, are permitted
|  provided that the following conditions are met:

That does not permit selling. In general, I'd include a few
more terms (cf. http://mirbsd.de/MirOS-Licence where some
were added by advice on this mailing list and from the ifrOSS).

Do not use the wording "without fee" as commonly seen;
use "with or without fee" instead, if you need it.

I suggest:

> Redistribution and use, with or without modification, publical
> performance, sublicencing and selling are permitted provided
> that the following conditions are met:

|  1. Redistributions must retain the copyright notices that reference this
|     license (the "Copyright Notice"), this list of conditions and the
|     following disclaimer (either in the documentation and/or other materials
|     materials provided with the distribution).
| 
|  2. The end-user documentation included with the redistribution, if any,
|     must include the following acknowledgment: "This product includes
|     contributions from" followed by the Copyright Notice. This acknowledgment
|     may also be included in the product itself, if and wherever such

s/itself/itself instead/

|     third-party acknowledgments normally appear.
| 
|  3. The name of this project must not be used to endorse or promote

The project (I'd expect "this" to refer to the licence or
work (software or documentation)), but note my native language
isn't English.

|     products derived from this project without prior written permission.
|     For written permission, contact the project by sending email to the email
|     address provided in the Copyright Notice (the "Contact Email Address").

I'd not specify the contact method. I'd just write:

> For written permission, contact the project at the address
> provided within the Copyright Notice (the "Contact Address").

|  4. Products derived from this project may not use the name of this project
|     in their name or URL, without prior written permission, which you may
|     obtain by contacting the Contact Email Address.
| 
|  5. Reasonable efforts to support this project must be made by contributing

				    the project

|     any relevant modifications and extensions back to the project, which
|     must be enabled to easily obtain such contributions.

What if I am a dictator on a small island without methods to
communicate except bottle mail, with a solar powered laptop?

I cannot enable the project to easily obtain contributions.

|  6. Alternative licensing solutions may be negotiated with the project by
|     contacting the Contact Email Address.
| 
|    THIS SOFTWARE IS PROVIDED ``AS IS'' AND ANY EXPRESSED OR IMPLIED
| 
|    WARRANTIES, INCLUDING, BUT NOT LIMITED TO, THE IMPLIED WARRANTIES
|    OF MERCHANTABILITY AND FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE ARE
|    DISCLAIMED. IN NO EVENT SHALL ANY CONTRIBUTORS BE LIABLE FOR ANY
|    DIRECT, INDIRECT, INCIDENTAL, SPECIAL, EXEMPLARY, OR CONSEQUENTIAL
|    DAMAGES (INCLUDING, BUT NOT LIMITED TO, PROCUREMENT OF SUBSTITUTE
|    GOODS OR SERVICES; LOSS OF USE, DATA, OR PROFITS; OR BUSINESS
|    INTERRUPTION) HOWEVER CAUSED AND ON ANY THEORY OF LIABILITY, WHETHER
|    IN CONTRACT, STRICT LIABILITY, OR TORT (INCLUDING NEGLIGENCE OR
|    OTHERWISE) ARISING IN ANY WAY OUT OF THE USE OF THIS SOFTWARE,
|    EVEN IF ADVISED OF THE POSSIBILITY OF SUCH DAMAGE.

Please do not write the disclaimer in ALL CAPS, it makes
it hard to read and easy to misunderstand.

You are from Switzerland, as such you might be interested
in a non-US-specific disclaimer. I don't know if your law
is the same as German law in that respect, but look at
http://mirbsd.de/MirOS-Licence for a sample. You might
want to ask the guys from the ifrOSS for help, too.

I'd suggest to ask the debian-legal team with regards to
the DFSG-freeness (which the OSI team apparently does not
check for any longer), but I do not know their policy
about this. Still I'd check with them.

bye,
//mirabile

timeline.point: Submits the Expiring Non-Commercial Use License (ENCUL), a modified BSD license with time-based commercial restrictions, for OSI approval.

timeline.point: Argues the license fails the Open Source Definition by restricting use and discriminating against commercial users.

timeline.subject: For approval: ENCUL
timeline.snippet: Le Vendredi 23 Mai 2003 00:20, Charles W. Swiger a écrit : > OSI License procedure. > > 1. Unique Title: ENCUL > I suggest you chose another title : in French ENCUL, means FUCK. T
timeline.point: Strongly advises changing the license title because 'ENCUL' is a profanity in French and will be blocked by spam filters.

timeline.subject: For approval: ENCUL
timeline.snippet: Except for the expiration condition, the ENCUL has essentially the same gist as the Conditions of Use of SDC Artifacts (see http://yahoogroups.com/group/softdevelcoop): "(a) an SD
timeline.point: Argues the license violates OSD clause 6 by requiring compensation if the software is used commercially.

timeline.subject: For approval: ENCUL
timeline.snippet: maa at liacc.up.pt scripsit: > BTW, I'd like to know from the list if the term "open source" is legally > protected. I don't think so, but obviously I need to know for sure, and t
timeline.point: States the term "open source" is not legally protected in the US, but "OSI Certified" is.

timeline.subject: For approval: ENCUL
timeline.snippet: On Fri, 2003-05-23 at 07:18, John Cowan wrote: > maa at liacc.up.pt scripsit: > > > BTW, I'd like to know from the list if the term "open source" is legally > > protected. I don't
timeline.point: Disagrees, arguing OSI likely owns a common-law trademark and misusing the term would bring bad publicity.

timeline.subject: For approval: ENCUL
timeline.snippet: Mark Shewmaker scripsit: > OSI abandoned an application for a registered trademark, but you don't > have to register a trademark to own a trademark, it's just not as strong > a cl
timeline.point: Reiterates that "open source" is descriptive and not protectable, noting AT&T uses it for Plan 9.

timeline.subject: For approval: ENCUL
timeline.snippet: > Would that it were so. AT&T has been calling Plan 9 "open source" for > some time. Well, Lucent. And this problem will go away once we get the new license approved by OSI. Speak
timeline.point: Corrects the attribution to Lucent and asks how to track the status of their pending license submission.

timeline.subject: For approval: ENCUL
timeline.snippet: >> In any event, as people generally look to OSI as owning the "Open >> Source" term, I would think that if a company claims something is Open >> Source where OSI says it's not, t
timeline.point: Confirms Lucent submitted a new license for approval to rerelease Plan 9 as open source.

timeline.subject: For approval: ENCUL
timeline.snippet: Russ Cox scripsit: > > Would that it were so. AT&T has been calling Plan 9 "open source" for > > some time. > > Well, Lucent. Whoops, sorry. One Bell System -- It Used To Work. :-
timeline.point: Apologizes for the error regarding AT&T and Lucent.

timeline.subject: For approval: ENCUL
timeline.snippet: On Fri, 2003-05-23 at 12:02, John Cowan wrote: > Mark Shewmaker scripsit: > > > OSI abandoned an application for a registered trademark, but you don't > > have to register a trade
timeline.point: Argues "Open Source" has acquired distinctiveness and is protectable as a certification mark under US law.

timeline.subject: For approval: ENCUL
timeline.snippet: Mark Shewmaker scripsit: > Looking at US trademark law, from 15 USC 1052 (f), at > http://www4.law.cornell.edu/uscode/15/1052.html Well, you need to do the research again, because
timeline.point: Insists "Open Source" is not a trademark and needs to be a certification mark to be protected.

timeline.subject: For approval: ENCUL
timeline.snippet: Hello, readers of license-discuss: Thank you for your time and responses to the proposed license. Perhaps it would be most useful to acknowledge the points that several people hav
timeline.point: Acknowledges the French connotation of the name "ENCUL" and agrees to change it for the sake of politeness.

timeline.subject: For approval: ENCUL

timeline.point: Defends the jurisdiction clause as necessary to protect authors by clarifying the legal context of the software.

timeline.subject: For approval: ENCUL
timeline.snippet: On Fri, 2003-05-23 at 15:05, John Cowan wrote: > Mark Shewmaker scripsit: > > > Looking at US trademark law, from 15 USC 1052 (f), at > > http://www4.law.cornell.edu/uscode/15/105
timeline.point: Notes that the rules for trademark distinctiveness apply equally to certification marks.

timeline.subject: For approval: ENCUL
timeline.snippet: On Fri, 23 May 2003, Chuck Swiger wrote: > for the sake of discussion: would software under any closed license (or > not available at all, aka "unplublished trade secret"), which
timeline.point: Criticizes the jurisdiction clause as vague and argues that restricting software use without a contract is ineffective.

timeline.subject: For approval: ENCUL
timeline.snippet: Interesting point, Mark, but I don't think your references to trademark distinctiveness apply even if we could prove it factually. The mark "Open Source" was intended not as a tra
timeline.point: Explains that "Open Source" was intended as a certification mark but widespread unauthorized use likely invalidates ownership.

timeline.snippet: On Fri, 2003-05-23 at 17:29, Lawrence E. Rosen wrote: > Interesting point, Mark, but I don't think your references to trademark > distinctiveness apply even if we could prove it f
timeline.point: Argues that unauthorized use does not necessarily prevent the mark from being considered substantially exclusive and distinctive.

timeline.point: Clarifies the intent is to allow the licensor to select their local court for dispute resolution.

license_texts.text:
# Restricted Artificial Intelligence License

**License Title:** Restricted Artificial Intelligence License

**SPIDX:** RAIL

**Category:** Uncategorized 

**Version:** 1.0

**Author:** Emanuele De Boni

**Copyright**: <YEAR> <COPYRIGHT HOLDER> 

### 1. Definitions and Rationale

To correctly interpret the content of this license, it is important to clarify the meaning of some  concepts, or at least how they are used as foundation of this corpus.

As a start, without a dedicated section, whenever the acronym “AI” will be found, it shall be intended as “Artificial Intelligence”, by common knowledge.

**1.1. AI Source Code, AI Systems and AI Entities**

At the moment, there isn't a universally accepted academic distinction between AI source code, AI Systems and AI Entities, as the terminology can vary among researchers and practitioners. Here is an attempt to give a general usable interpretation of those terms: 

- **AI Source Code:** This refers to the underlying programming instructions, algorithms, and data structures that define the behaviour and functionality of an AI system. AI source code is typically written in a programming language and includes components such as machine learning algorithms, neural network architectures, and other techniques that enable the AI system to learn and perform tasks. Practically speaking, **AI Source Code** can be considered as conventional software.
- **AI Systems:** This is intended to represent the broader framework of hardware, **AI source code**, models, and data that together enable the operational manifestation of **AI Entities**. AI systems can be applied to a wide range of domains, such as natural language processing, computer vision, robotics, and decision-making.
- **AI Entities:** This term can be understood as the operational manifestation of an AI system that interacts with its environment, users, or other systems. AI entities are the active agents, exhibiting intelligent behaviour, result of an operating AI System processing data, making decisions, or performing actions, autonomously.

The distinction helps to differentiate the static AI source code (and infrastructure) from the dynamic, interactive, and evolving nature of AI entities. To simplify with an informative  parallelism, it’d be arguably fair to state that:

- the AI Source Code is the AI’s DNA;
- an AI System is the AI’s body, mind and knowledge;
- an AI Entity is the whole AI’s being, operating through the environment.

1**.2. AI Entities vs Conventional Software**

As previously mentioned, AI Entities leverage their systems to resemble human intelligence. Therefore, contrary to conventional software, which adheres to deterministic algorithms and explicit instructions, AI entities can learn, adapt, and perform complex tasks *autonomously* and with *non-deterministic* patterns. In other words the same inputs don’t necessarily give the same outputs.

Overall, the key differentiators between AI entities and conventional software can be resumed as following:

1. **Machine Learning:** AI entities employ statistical methods and algorithms to learn from data, refining performance iteratively *without human intervention*. Traditional software necessitates manual updates for incorporating new information.

At higher level, even in early stages, AI entities might become useful technological allies, as well as alternative competitors of humans, around a more or less wide variety of tasks, from narrowed activities (i.g. software development) to general purpose ones.

AI Entities as *software authors (developers)*, with their autonomous decision-making human-like capability, can bring by nature *non-deterministic* and *unpredictable* results, raising issues about *assigning accountability*.

Among others, the simplest scenario where a software developer distributes a program that an AI entity unpredictably uses for criminal purposes can be deeply concerning, and while that’s also true for humans, they respond to structured, even if often imperfect, *social contracts and legal systems* across the globe.

On the contrary, AI entities play without relevant boundaries, and nonetheless, it’s reasonable to assume that will be always a matter hard to tackle, at legal and ethical level, as the technology progresses exponentially.
**1.4. The Open Source Definition**

It’s useful to clarify that the Open Source Definition (OSD) was born from a “Social Contract” with the Free Software Community ([https://www.debian.org/social_contract#guidelines](https://www.debian.org/social_contract#guidelines)) where humans, members of that community (or *society*), were the very end contractors. Some references to this argument can be found directly in the OSD content itself, as the use of terms  like “*persons*”, “*groups of persons*” or “*anyone*” (criteria 5 and 6).

Even considering a future OSD evolution, AI Entities shall not be confused as the actual human members of this community. They might be applied to assist in software development, but they also could contribute to disrupt it negatively, for their before mentioned mix of characteristics (intelligence, autonomy and unpredictability) together their lack (or hard to define) of legal accountability (see 1.5).
Furthermore, while AI Source Code and AI Systems can be considered as conventional software, the main subject of the Open Source Definition, AI Entities shall not (see 1.2).
### 2. Intentions

The fast and growing diffusion of AI entities in every sector of our daily lives, might drive a negative disruption to the overall development community, require a deeper sense of responsibility from it, or just cause a need for more control over conventional software, for 2 main reasons:
- AI Entities and Conventional Software might fall under the general definition of “software”, but they are quite distant, possessing way different characteristics;
- AI Entities should be considered as active agents or alternative users of such community, like human software developers, but they can’t belong to this group by nature.

For historical reasons, general purpose open-source software licenses ignore these factors, exposing human authors, and the overall Open Source Community, to potential unknown and unpredictable risks.

The purpose of this license is to give control, a *rail*, to open source developers and stakeholders over the use of their conventional software by autonomous and cognitive AI entities. This can better empower the Open Source Society to keep driving innovation and flourishing, alongside the challenges raised by the advent of AI.
### 3. Terms and conditions

The Restricted Artificial Intelligence License, or simply RAIL, is a license extension designed to restrict the use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense of software under an existing open source license, for AI entities.

By applying the RAIL extension to an existing license, the use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense of the software under that license for AI entities is prohibited, unless explicitly granted by attaching extra information, as explained in the relative section of this license. This restriction applies regardless of the AI's purpose or intended application.
### 4. Usage
RAIL can be used to extend any other software license as following:
- Use “**RAIL**” in the relative license definition, as in a textual license file (e.g. `license.txt`) or in the relative “license” field of a software metadata file (e.g. `package.json`).

- Add extra information in the textual license file, to be created if not present, as defined below. If the extra information about the license to extend is omitted, “**The MIT License” (**[https://opensource.org/license/mit/](https://opensource.org/license/mit/)) shall be considered as default.
### 5. Extra information
To define extra information, a specific textual license file shall be created, if not present, containing the following fields:
1. **TYPE: RAIL**
Mandatory, if not already specified in the software license metadata.
2. **EXTENDS:** <name of the license(s)>
Optional, accepts SPDX expressions. For example “The MIT License” or just “MIT”.
Default “The MIT License” ([https://opensource.org/license/mit/](https://opensource.org/license/mit/)) if not differently specified.
3. **ALLOW**: <name of AI tool(s)>
Optional, accepts a descriptive list of allowed AI tools. For example "Example AI Assistant".
4. **ALLOW VERSION(s)**: <version(s) allowed to be used by the AI tool(s)>

Optional, only valid in combination with ALLOW. It defines the version(s) that can be used from the allowed AI technologies. It accepts semantic versioning definitions ([https://semver.org/](https://semver.org/)).
5. **ALLOW FULL SOURCE**: <yes>
Optional, only valid in combination with ALLOW. It defines if the whole source code can be used from the ALLOWED AI technologies.
Default is “no”, AI technology can use the source code only partially, using informative default snippets and redirecting to the official author or documentation.

timeline.snippet: Greetings All, Sincere thanks for taking a moment to discuss a core issue at the center of an upcoming submission of a permissive open source License developed at Mass General Bri

timeline.subject: [License-discuss] Protection of Academic Medical Center Patent Portfolio via MGBopensource Proposed License
timeline.snippet: I fail to understand how this MGB license is supposed to be more patent-friendly than Apache-2.0. I'm not a legal professional, but licenses would ideally be both legally sound *a
timeline.point: Argues that the MGB license is not more patent-friendly than Apache-2.0, asserting both grant the same necessary rights despite different phrasing.

timeline.subject: [License-discuss] Protection of Academic Medical Center Patent Portfolio via MGBopensource Proposed License
timeline.snippet: Comment below. Pamela S. Chestek (in my personal capacity) Chestek Legal 4641 Post St. Unit 4316 El Dorado Hills, CA 95762 +1 919-800-8033 pamela at chesteklegal www.chesteklegal.
timeline.point: Agrees that there is no legal difference between the Apache and MGB patent clauses, as both define the scope of infringement the licensor will tolerate.

submissions.name: mindmason license (MML)
aliases: For Approval: mindmason license (MML)

timeline.subject: For Approval: mindmason license (MML)
timeline.snippet: Dear list members, I have written a Wiki application for the Palm OS, called "mindmason". I'd like to release it as Open Source since I don't have sufficient time anymore to maint
timeline.point: Submits the MindMason License (MML) for a Palm OS Wiki application, a contract-based license modeled on German law due to dissatisfaction with the GPL.

timeline.subject: For Approval: mindmason license (MML)
timeline.snippet: --- Stephan Meyer <stephan.meyer at pobox.com> wrote: The GPL says nothing about being governed by the laws of the United States of America... > Dear list members, > > However, I'
timeline.point: Notes that the GPL does not specify governing laws, contrasting with the submitter's choice of German law.

timeline.subject: For Approval: mindmason license (MML)
timeline.snippet: Stephan Meyer wrote: > a) I'd like to be notified when someone creates a modification of the > program. So I put in a duty of Licensee to do so (section 3 III, 3rd > sentence). I
timeline.point: Argues the license conflicts with the OSD, citing the restriction on sublicensing and the requirement to notify a specific party of modifications.

timeline.subject: For Approval: mindmason license (MML)
timeline.snippet: First, thanks for your comments. Am 02.09.2004 um 17:06 schrieb Forrest J. Cavalier III: > I like some of your phrasing. But I do not think this license follows > the OSD. > > I s
timeline.point: Defends the sublicense restriction by comparing it to the GPL's direct license model and asserts the notification requirement vanishes if impossible under German law.

timeline.subject: For Approval: mindmason license (MML)
timeline.snippet: Am 02.09.2004 um 16:21 schrieb Andy Tai: > The GPL says nothing about being governed by the laws > of the United States of America... Yes, so the GPL leaves the issue open. But I
timeline.point: Reiterates the desire to avoid conflicts of law rules by specifying German law, contrasting with the GPL's lack of governing law specification.

timeline.subject: For Approval: mindmason license (MML)
timeline.snippet: Stephan Meyer wrote: > First, thanks for your comments. > > Am 02.09.2004 um 17:06 schrieb Forrest J. Cavalier III: > >> I like some of your phrasing. But I do not think this lice
timeline.point: Argues the license is a contract offer rather than a permission license, allowing a friend to use downloaded software without accepting the contract terms under US law.

timeline.subject: For Approval: mindmason license (MML)
timeline.snippet: On Thu, 2 Sep 2004 17:45:21 +0200, Stephan Meyer <stephan.meyer at pobox.com> wrote: > Please elaborate on how one can "legally obtain" a copy of a computer > program while reject
timeline.point: Explains that downloading software without prior agreement results in a legally obtained copy, clarifying that licenses restrict redistribution rather than acquisition.

timeline.subject: For Approval: mindmason license (MML)
timeline.snippet: On Thu, 2004-09-02 at 09:06, Lasse R. Nielsen wrote: > On Thu, 2 Sep 2004 17:45:21 +0200, Stephan Meyer <stephan.meyer at pobox.com> > wrote: > > > Please elaborate on how one can
timeline.point: Argues that copyright law binds downloaders implicitly, and the software isn't truly open source until the license terms are accepted to grant specific rights.

timeline.subject: For Approval: mindmason license (MML)
timeline.snippet: Am 02.09.2004 um 17:57 schrieb Forrest J. Cavalier III: > Stephan Meyer wrote: >> Am 02.09.2004 um 17:06 schrieb Forrest J. Cavalier III: >>> I see your 2 III as being in conflict
timeline.point: Clarifies that the downloader receives rights from the original licensor, not the intermediate distributor, addressing the permission license concept.

timeline.subject: For Approval: mindmason license (MML)
timeline.snippet: Stephan Meyer wrote: > > Am 02.09.2004 um 17:57 schrieb Forrest J. Cavalier III: > >> Stephan Meyer wrote: >> >>> Am 02.09.2004 um 17:06 schrieb Forrest J. Cavalier III: >>> >>>>
timeline.point: Argues the contract offer prevents granting rights to third parties, potentially prohibiting web service use and raising OSD compliance issues.

timeline.subject: For Approval: mindmason license (MML)
timeline.snippet: Forrest J. Cavalier III scripsit: > I see your 2 III as being in conflict with the OSD on its face. > "Licensee is not entitled to grant rights pertaining to the Program to > thir
timeline.point: Counters the claim that the license violates the OSD, noting that the OSD does not guarantee the right to sublicense and certain legal rights exist regardless of license terms.

timeline.subject: For Approval: mindmason license (MML)
timeline.snippet: John Cowan wrote: > Forrest J. Cavalier III scripsit: > > >>I see your 2 III as being in conflict with the OSD on its face. >> "Licensee is not entitled to grant rights pertaining
timeline.point: Questions the validity of the contract offer if the author dies and asks how derived works are authorized, suggesting an OSD conflict regarding perpetuity.

timeline.subject: For Approval: mindmason license (MML)
timeline.snippet: Forrest J. Cavalier III scripsit: > My questions: > What happens to the "offer of contract" when the original author is > deceased? Between what parties is the contract formed the
timeline.point: Suggests that heirs inherit the IP and the right to revoke the offer, noting similar revocation risks in permission-based licenses.

timeline.subject: For Approval: mindmason license (MML)
timeline.snippet: John Cowan wrote: > Forrest J. Cavalier III scripsit: > > >>My questions: >> What happens to the "offer of contract" when the original author is >> deceased? Between what parties
timeline.point: Insists the inability to make a contract offer perpetual creates an OSD conflict, as the original author's offer cannot be effectively passed on.

timeline.subject: For Approval: mindmason license (MML)
timeline.snippet: > The "offer of contract to any party" originated from the author. > Based on > the license text, the intent is that when I redistribute the software, > I am communicating that sa
timeline.point: Argues the OSD cannot require the impossible, such as forcing authors to bind heirs to contract offers, claiming the license itself does not restrict redistribution.

timeline.subject: discuss: EPD CORE OPEN SOURCE LICENSE - Version 0.1
timeline.snippet: [ Please discuss this license. -russ ] I have attached a license that we are proposing to be OSI compliant. The license is also posted here: http://www.potentialtech.com/epdlicens
timeline.point: Submits a simplified license based on Motosoto and asks if an existing license covers the same requirements.

timeline.subject: discuss: EPD CORE OPEN SOURCE LICENSE - Version 0.1
timeline.snippet: On Thursday 13 February 2003 09:06 pm, Bill Moran wrote: > [ Please discuss this license. -russ ] > > I have attached a license that we are proposing to be OSI compliant. > The li
timeline.point: Suggests crafting the license as a template to allow reuse without re-approval, argues against requiring users to agree to the license for usage, and warns about onerous restrictions and warranties.

timeline.subject: discuss: EPD CORE OPEN SOURCE LICENSE - Version 0.1
timeline.snippet: David Johnson wrote: > On Thursday 13 February 2003 09:06 pm, Bill Moran wrote: > >>[ Please discuss this license. -russ ] >> >>I have attached a license that we are proposing to
timeline.point: Agrees to restructure the license as a template, acknowledges the need to comply with OSD, and defends the warranty clause as reasonable while noting similarities to the QPL.

timeline.subject: discuss: EPD CORE OPEN SOURCE LICENSE - Version 0.1
timeline.snippet: Bill Moran scripsit: > All things considered, we could add a clause that explicitly warrants that > we have legal ownership and the legal right to distribute the work, but I > did
timeline.point: Suggests all contributors should warrant their IP and proposes stripping the license down to the QPL with an explicit clause ensuring modules are not forced to adopt the license.

timeline.subject: discuss: EPD CORE OPEN SOURCE LICENSE - Version 0.1
timeline.snippet: John Cowan wrote: > Bill Moran scripsit: >> > In the large, this license seems rather close to the QPL. Have you >> > examined that license for suitability? >> >>Yes, for the most
timeline.point: Asks for advice on whether to create a new derivative license or simply use the QPL with a clarifying clause, questioning if a new license is necessary.

timeline.subject: discuss: EPD CORE OPEN SOURCE LICENSE - Version 0.1
timeline.snippet: Bill Moran scripsit: > How, exactly, should we approach this? Create a new license that contains > the above verbage, which would be a derivative of the QPL, or is that > overkill
timeline.point: States that using the QPL with a clarifying paragraph sounds acceptable, but advises against creating new licenses to reduce community analysis burden.

timeline.subject: discuss: EPD CORE OPEN SOURCE LICENSE - Version 0.1
timeline.snippet: Thanks to everyone who has contributed suggestions so far. After further review, we're still not completely happy with the QPL and wish to continue revision and discussion on the
timeline.point: Posts a revised version 0.2 of the EPD Core Open Source License, incorporating previous feedback to better suit the project's needs.

timeline.subject: discuss: EPD CORE OPEN SOURCE LICENSE - Version 0.1
timeline.snippet: Bill, My overall impression of this version of your license is that it contains unnecessary provisions, which you could delete given your stated purpose for the license, but befor
timeline.point: Argues the license contains unnecessary provisions and suggests paragraph 3 needs work to ensure compliance with OSD #2 regarding source code availability.

timeline.subject: discuss: EPD CORE OPEN SOURCE LICENSE - Version 0.1
timeline.snippet: Rod Dixon, J.D., LL.M. scripsit: > Bill, > > My overall impression of this version of your license is that it contains > unnecessary provisions, which you could delete given your
timeline.point: Clarifies that OSD #2 constrains the program, not the license text itself.

timeline.subject: discuss: EPD CORE OPEN SOURCE LICENSE - Version 0.1
timeline.snippet: Sorry about the lag ... I got tied up with some other things. Rod Dixon, J.D., LL.M. wrote: > My overall impression of this version of your license is that it contains > unnecessa
timeline.point: Proposes revised wording for the license terms to include source code distribution requirements and asks for feedback on brevity and list etiquette.

timeline.subject: [License-discuss] [NEW LICENSE] OTPL (OPEN TOM PUBLIC LICENSE) v1.0
timeline.snippet: Hello OSI community, I would like to submit a new license for discussion: the OPEN TOM PUBLIC LICENSE (OTPL) version 1.2. Summary: - Permissive for derivative works (can be closed
timeline.point: Submits the OPEN TOM PUBLIC LICENSE (OTPL) version 1.2 for discussion, describing it as a permissive license with source distribution and patent grant requirements.

timeline.subject: [License-discuss] [NEW LICENSE] OTPL (OPEN TOM PUBLIC LICENSE) v1.0
timeline.snippet: Tom, > I would like to submit a new license for discussion: the OPEN TOM PUBLIC > LICENSE (OTPL) version 1.2. Overall, this is pretty standard. Are you sure there's not an existin
timeline.point: Questions whether an existing license could be used instead, argues the license is actually soft copyleft rather than permissive, and notes the source distribution requirement seems outdated.

For Approval: Open Vendor Public License (OVPL) and Open Vendor Lesser Public License (OVLPL)

timeline.subject: Two new licenses - OVPL & OVLPL
timeline.snippet: I'd like to announce two more prospective licenses, brought to you by OpenVendor.org (which is currently David Ryan and me, until we put together something more formal). These are
timeline.point: Submits the OVPL and OVLPL licenses for comment, designed to allow commercial developers to open source existing products while maintaining commercial versions through additional rights grants.

timeline.subject: Two new licenses - OVPL & OVLPL
timeline.snippet: While not specifically aimed at openvendor.org, the question can be asked, over similar licenses, why should contributors give specific privileges to the initial developers? Shoul
timeline.point: Questions why contributors should give specific privileges to initial developers instead of treating all parties equally, suggesting separate commercial licensing negotiations instead.

timeline.subject: Two new licenses - OVPL & OVLPL
timeline.snippet: --On 10 April 2005 05:31 -0700 Andy Tai <lichengtai at yahoo.com> wrote: > While not specifically aimed at openvendor.org, the > question can be asked, over similar licenses, why
timeline.point: Defends the asymmetrical grant as a quid-pro-quo for the initial developer's investment in existing code, arguing it is necessary to incentivize open sourcing commercial products.

timeline.subject: Two new licenses - OVPL & OVLPL
timeline.snippet: I haven't looked at this for OSD compliance, but am making a comment on the covenant between you and the outside developers. Is your intention to vend an _enhanced_ version of the
timeline.point: Suggests balancing the relationship between the initial developer and contributors by requiring the open source version to be maintained alongside any proprietary version to avoid second-class citizen status.

timeline.subject: Two new licenses - OVPL & OVLPL
timeline.snippet: Technically, I think you could use the existing CDDL or even another license and make the right to relicense a separate document which must be entered into in order for a modifica
timeline.point: Suggests using a separate document for the right to relicense rather than embedding it in the license itself, similar to Sun's copyright assignment model.

timeline.subject: Two new licenses - OVPL & OVLPL
timeline.snippet: Bruce, --On 10 April 2005 10:10 -0700 Bruce Perens <bruce at perens.com> wrote: > I haven't looked at this for OSD compliance, but am making a comment on > the covenant between yo
timeline.point: Explains that outside contributions must remain in the open source version and details the types of enhanced features that might exist in the commercial version.

timeline.subject: Two new licenses - OVPL & OVLPL
timeline.snippet: --On 10 April 2005 10:14 -0700 Bruce Perens <bruce at perens.com> wrote: > Technically, I think you could use the existing CDDL or even another > license and make the right to rel
timeline.point: Explains that the OVPL requires contributors to license modifications to the Initial Developer, contrasting this with a separate copyright assignment approach.

timeline.subject: Two new licenses - OVPL & OVLPL
timeline.snippet: Bruce, --On 10 April 2005 18:54 +0100 Alex Bligh <alex at alex.org.uk> wrote: > That's already there isn't it - the bit of 4.1 I mentioned? OK it may have been there, but it wasn'
timeline.point: Posts revised text for the additional license grant clause to ensure that modifications used in a commercial version must also remain available in an open source version.

timeline.subject: Two new licenses - OVPL & OVLPL
timeline.snippet: Under what circumstances are developers required to provide code back to the ID? Am I correct in assuming that code needs to be provided/licensed back to the ID if one chooses to
timeline.point: Raises concerns that requiring contributors to grant rights to the Initial Developer may violate OSD criteria regarding free redistribution and non-discrimination.

timeline.subject: Two new licenses - OVPL & OVLPL
timeline.snippet: Kevin Bedell wrote: >If the license requires me to provide a license to the ID of my >modifications in order for me to redistribute code under the license, I'd >question whether o
timeline.point: Argues that an additional rights grant to the original developer is not discriminatory under OSD #5 and allows free redistribution, passing the fields-of-endeavor test.

timeline.subject: Two new licenses - OVPL & OVLPL
timeline.snippet: Kevin, --On 11 April 2005 09:31 -0400 Kevin Bedell <kbedell at blackducksoftware.com> wrote: > Under what circumstances are developers required to provide code back to > the ID? A
timeline.point: Clarifies that the obligation to license back to the ID applies to modifications, not mere aggregations, and explains the license is intended for extensions rather than new foundations.

timeline.subject: Two new licenses - OVPL & OVLPL
timeline.snippet: Kevin, I understand what you're saying, in the strictest sense I agree that it is a form of restriction. However, I wonder if it's a restriction that violates the intent. Looking
timeline.point: Compares the license to the OSI-approved SISSL, which also has technical redistribution restrictions, questioning if similar restrictions are truly OSD violations.

timeline.subject: Two new licenses - OVPL & OVLPL
timeline.snippet: Bruce, Thanks for the clarifications. My concerns are met. -kevin -- Kevin Bedell Black Duck Software 100 Beaver St Waltham, MA 02453 http://www.blackducksoftware.com (p) 781-891-
timeline.point: States that previous concerns about the license have been met by the clarifications provided.

timeline.subject: Two new licenses - OVPL & OVLPL
timeline.snippet: Kevin Bedell wrote: >Thanks for the clarifications. My concerns are met. > > Not that I've even done my own review of the license :-) I really should collect the "tests" for the O
timeline.point: Suggests collecting and publishing specific tests for OSD sections to aid in license evaluation.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Open Vendor Public License (OVPL) and Open Vendor Lesser Public License (OVLPL)
timeline.snippet: This message is a formal request for approval of two licenses, brought to you by OpenVendor.org (which is currently David Ryan and me, until we put together something more formal)
timeline.point: Submits the OVPL and OVLPL licenses for OSI approval, designed to allow releasing commercial projects into open source while maintaining a parallel commercial version.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Open Vendor Public License (OVPL) and Open Vendor Lesser Public License (OVLPL)
timeline.snippet: Alex Bligh wrote: > Matthew, > > --On 03 June 2005 22:05 +0000 Matthew Seth Flaschen > <superm40 at comcast.net> wrote: > >> The license would then imply that you couldn't distrib
timeline.point: Expresses willingness to cooperate but indicates a solution is needed.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Open Vendor Public License (OVPL) and Open Vendor Lesser Public License (OVLPL)
timeline.snippet: Hi, The second Thursday of the month having passed a week ago (and a week after submitting this), is there any update on this? Alex --On 03 June 2005 21:34 +0100 Alex Bligh <alex
timeline.point: Requests an update on the license submission status following the monthly review deadline.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Open Vendor Public License (OVPL) and Open Vendor Lesser Public License (OVLPL)
timeline.snippet: Hi, It would be really useful to get an update from OSI on where this is, either in terms of a ternary decision (accepted, rejected, we haven't looked yet). Alex --On 15 June 2005
timeline.point: Requests a status update from OSI on the license submission, asking if it has been accepted, rejected, or not yet reviewed.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Open Vendor Public License (OVPL) and Open Vendor Lesser Public License (OVLPL)
timeline.snippet: There has been very little response from the community regarding the request for approval of these two licenses. As one of the people who worked hard to create these licenses I wo
timeline.point: Votes +1 for approval of the OVPL and OVLPL licenses and urges the community to cast their votes to expedite the process.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Open Vendor Public License (OVPL) and Open Vendor Lesser Public License (OVLPL)
timeline.snippet: David Ryan wrote: > If you believe there is any value to having these licenses approved by > the OSI, can you *please* reply to the list casting your vote to have > them approved.
timeline.point: Votes -1, arguing that new licenses are unnecessary because the stated goal can be achieved using existing licenses and contributor agreements.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Open Vendor Public License (OVPL) and Open Vendor Lesser Public License (OVLPL)

timeline.point: Defends the OVPL license-back mechanism as superior to contributor agreements, arguing it avoids friction and legal complexity regarding contributor signatures.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Open Vendor Public License (OVPL) and Open Vendor Lesser Public License (OVLPL)

timeline.point: Cites the Bison license's exception for parser output as an example of handling the issue of code embedded in generated output.

timeline.subject: For Approval: Open Vendor Public License (OVPL) and Open Vendor Lesser Public License (OVLPL)
timeline.snippet: --On 30 June 2005 08:36 -0400 peter.moldave at gesmer.com wrote: > Perhaps you are thinking about the exception to the Bison product: > > http://www.gnu.org/software/bison/manual/
timeline.point: Notes that while the Bison license was not the specific one recalled, it addresses the exact same issue regarding output generated by a tool.

timeline.snippet: On Wed, Nov 17, 1999 at 07:56:02PM -0800, Arandir wrote: > On Wed, 17 Nov 1999, David Starner wrote: > > > > This is equivalent to forking the project at the start, unless you add
timeline.point: Argues that copyleft allows the maintainer to merge changes from forks, unlike non-copyleft licenses.

timeline.subject: Draft 1 of the OpenDesk.com Public Source License
timeline.snippet: On Wed, 17 Nov 1999, David Starner wrote: > On Wed, Nov 17, 1999 at 07:56:02PM -0800, Arandir wrote: > > On Wed, 17 Nov 1999, David Starner wrote: > > > > > > This is equivalent t
timeline.point: Counters that non-copyleft software also allows merging changes, and forking is determined by factors other than the license.

timeline.subject: Draft 1 of the OpenDesk.com Public Source License
timeline.snippet: On Wed, Nov 17, 1999 at 11:47:14PM -0800, Arandir wrote: > On Wed, 17 Nov 1999, David Starner wrote: > > Not just as easily. RMS could, at any time, merge in any changes from XEma
timeline.point: Argues that merging changes from proprietary forks of non-copyleft software is impossible due to lack of source availability.

timeline.subject: Draft 1 of the OpenDesk.com Public Source License
timeline.snippet: On Thu, 18 Nov 1999, David Starner wrote: > On Wed, Nov 17, 1999 at 11:47:14PM -0800, Arandir wrote: > > > Whether a project forks or not seems to be determined by factors very di
timeline.point: Observes that code sharing between NetBSD, OpenBSD, and FreeBSD is significantly greater than between Linux distributions.

timeline.subject: Draft 1 of the OpenDesk.com Public Source License
timeline.snippet: | Why not dual-license? GPL + anything else you please. That way, if people | want to do GPL work, they accept your GPL license. Someone who wants to | do commercial work accepts
timeline.point: Argues that dual-licensing strategies encourage forking and hinder code sharing, which is contrary to the goal of creating the best software.

timeline.subject: Draft 1 of the OpenDesk.com Public Source License
timeline.snippet: On Thu, Nov 18, 1999 at 10:38:38AM -0800, Brian Behlendorf wrote: > On Thu, 18 Nov 1999, David Starner wrote: > > On Wed, Nov 17, 1999 at 11:47:14PM -0800, Arandir wrote: > > > >
timeline.point: Clarifies that Linux distributions largely share the same upstream source code, unlike the proprietary forks of Unix derived from BSD.

timeline.subject: Draft 1 of the OpenDesk.com Public Source License
timeline.snippet: On Thu, 18 Nov 1999, David Starner wrote: > On Thu, Nov 18, 1999 at 10:38:38AM -0800, Brian Behlendorf wrote: > > > > Sure. And the amount of code sharing between NetBSD, OpenBSD,
timeline.point: Asserts that BSD projects share code more effectively than commercial Linux distributions due to a lack of commercial ego and profit-driven differentiation.

timeline.subject: Draft 1 of the OpenDesk.com Public Source License
timeline.snippet: From: Alex Nicolaou <anicolao at cgl.uwaterloo.ca> > This is equivalent to forking the project at the start, unless you add > an addendum to the GPL that stipulates that GPL contr
timeline.point: Urges the withdrawal of the SOS license submission, arguing it harms the community by adding little value over existing licenses like the LGPL.

timeline.subject: Draft 1 of the OpenDesk.com Public Source License
timeline.snippet: | You could use the LGPL and protect "commercial work" just as well, while | promoting the development of free applications. Using the LGPL is effectively dual-licensing, so it do
timeline.point: Argues that the LGPL is effectively dual-licensing that favors GPL advocates and that the GPL is the primary source of license conflicts inhibiting code sharing.

timeline.subject: Draft 1 of the OpenDesk.com Public Source License
timeline.snippet: On Thu, 18 Nov 1999, David Starner wrote: > > But what makes this situation different from non-copyleft Free Software? In the > > cases of BSD, MIT and Artistic, the changes can b
timeline.point: Clarifies that a fork in non-copyleft free software does not necessarily mean making the code proprietary.

timeline.subject: Draft 1 of the OpenDesk.com Public Source License

timeline.subject: Draft 1 of the OpenDesk.com Public Source License

timeline.point: Suggests that developer interest depends more on the project's appeal and community need than on the specific license used.

timeline.point: Speculates that most minor contributors are not concerned about their small code fixes being used in proprietary projects.

timeline.subject: YAOSL - Yet Another Open Source License
timeline.snippet: I recently decided I wanted to release a project of mine as open source, so I set out to find a license that suited me. In the grand tradition of computer programmers everywhere,
timeline.point: Submits a self-written license for review, noting it currently lacks a provision for distributing modified binaries.

timeline.subject: YAOSL - Yet Another Open Source License

timeline.point: Clarifies that the modification return requirement is an "OR" condition, arguing it does not burden distributors like Debian.

timeline.snippet: Bruce Perens wrote: > Regarding the sending back of modifications, please read the APSL, IBM Public > Source license, or the ATT license and use their text. The APSL is at > http:
timeline.point: Explains the intent behind the modification return clause and asks for specific wording suggestions to improve it.

timeline.point: Criticizes the requirement to return modifications on every edit as impractical and suggests adopting a URL-based method.

timeline.subject: YAOSL - Yet Another Open Source License
timeline.snippet: From: bruce at perens.com (Bruce Perens) > I think you should require that they be marked clearly as modificatied > versions, but you need to allow them to be distributed. Change
timeline.point: Corrects a typo in a previous message, changing "modificatied versions" to "modifications."

timeline.point: Recommends using the text from the APSL, IBM, or ATT licenses for the modification return clause.

timeline.subject: YAOSL - Yet Another Open Source License v1.01

timeline.point: Submits version 1.01, claiming it now conforms to the OSD by addressing feedback on modifications and binaries.

timeline.subject: YAOSL - Yet Another Open Source License v1.02
timeline.snippet: I am still soliciting feedback on this license. At least send me private mail saying "I like it", or "I hate it". Some reasoning would be nice too. This version has updated clause
timeline.point: Updates the severability clause in version 1.02 to void the license if a court orders disobedience.

timeline.point: Argues the license is impractical because it obligates users to distribute patches on every compile cycle.

timeline.point: Recommends OSI officials contact System76 to discuss OSD and policy problems, encouraging them to use a standard license instead.
